Senses.Explanation: A long sword reaching the sky names an outsized sword image used through explicit comparisons and predicates. Wuyi Yuanlai says that ‘this one thought’ is like the sword (這一念子如倚天長劍): anything touching its edge cannot be got at all, while lingering and grinding it dull means the sword has long been gone. Yuanwu Keqin describes the sword with ‘stern, awe-inspiring power’ (凜凜神威) and pairs it with the clear radiance of the sun. Yulin Tongxiu raises his staff and answers, ‘the sky-reaching long sword chills the person before it’ (倚天長劍逼人寒). Lianfeng Su imagines a person holding it and cutting eighty-one fascicles of ‘tangled vines’ like one skein, ‘one cut, all severed’ (將八十一卷爛葛藤如斬一綟絲，一斬一切斷). In the sole retained lamp witness, Ganlu Deyong compares Deshan Xuanjian’s blow to the sword and Linji Yixuan’s phrase to thunder on dry ground, then calls both ‘relying on force and raising waves without wind’ (盡是倚勢欺人無風起浪). These passages establish the towering sword, its edge, its power, its cold, and its cutting; they do not assign every sword occurrence one further meaning.

SearchAliases: the entire body is an eye
Senses.Explanation: The whole body is eyes is a stock Chan formula that makes the entire body the stated organ of seeing. Chan records make the whole body an organ of seeing, commonly beside whole-body hearing, speaking, or acting. Yuanwu says, 'the whole body is eyes, yet seeing does not reach it,' and extends the same construction to ears, mouth, and mind. Another discourse pairs 'the whole body is a mouth' with 'the whole body is eyes,' then assigns the former speech and the latter use. In public questioning, 'the Great Compassionate One does not extend a hand; the whole body is eyes' answers the class 'meaning and phrase both arrive.' Later case comments use the phrase as an appraisal of Yuanwu Keqin and as wording that itself still requires investigation.
